column2: height of the windway exit of alto d-: not published (only its length); the recipe uses 1.8 mm / 1.7 from two other sources. Windway heights of historic recorders are hard to measure (warping, crescent shape) and Bouterse gives no table
column5: onset pressure, register selection and every jet claim
column6: a measured windway of alto d- or a CT scan; a measured modern tenor recorder head (Price et al. 2015, ledger price-2015-recorder-jet-reflection) has a windway 1.95 mm high at the inlet and 1.09 mm at the exit, 72.0 mm long, with the lip 4.83 mm from the exit: the same order as this estimate

column2: curvature of the windway roof and labium edge (crescent shaped opening), direction of the roof (rising, axial, descending), width profile, chamfers, ovality; the recipe has a straight rectangular slit of constant height

offset of the jet axis from the labium edge: the step (0.8 mm) and the edge thickness are published but the jet position follows from the unknown windway height; the recipe takes the DERIVED mid-face value +0.1455 mm on the pipe side (edge underside step - h/2 = 0.2705 mm on the bore side, plus half the 0.25 mm face; ledger recorder-labium-offset-bouterse2010-derived) and jet angle zero
column3: face [0.0000205, 0.0002705] m at the estimated windway height (both ends rendered); with u-windway-height [0.5, 1.8] mm the mid-face spans [-0.000225, 0.000425] m

column2: position of hole 7 on the foot: only its diameter (5.0 to 5.5 mm) and the outer diameter of the foot there (32.0 mm) are published. The recipe opens it 24 mm below the foot's upper end (the DERIVED dimensions row); the lower bound is the 16.0 mm tenon socket plus the hole's radius, the upper bound an estimate of where the 32.0 mm bulb ends
column3: [0.018, 0.030] m below the upper end of the foot
column5: pitch of the notes with hole 7 open (a1, bb1, b1) and the foot's cross-fingerings
column6: a drawing or photograph of the foot (Morgan drawing X)

column2: undercutting of the finger holes (usual on Bressan altos, not stated for alto d-): none in the recipe
shrinkage and warping of the boxwood (oval bores, minima 0.2 to 0.4 mm smaller than the tabulated maxima), possible later repairs; the recipe uses the tabulated maxima
the half-closed thumb hole that gives the second and third registers is not modelled; only first-register notes are rendered
column5: all notes above the first register

column2: temperature of the air in the bore: the recipe uses the woodwind breath law, saturated breath at 27 C as the mean bore temperature of a played instrument (Nederveen, Acoustical aspects of woodwind instruments, 1969, sec. 12; Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, sec. 8.1; Coltman, JASA 40, 1966), the same law as the clarinet recipes. Bouterse's pitch measurements were made in rooms at 15 to 27 C, which brackets the temperature toward the open end; the recipe has one uniform gas, no temperature gradient along the bore
column5: absolute pitch: about 40 cents between the bracket ends (saturated air at 15 C against 27 C)

column2: carbon dioxide in the breath that fills the bore: the recipe takes the published composition of exhaled breath in a played woodwind, 4.5 % CO2 and 16.5 % O2 dry at 27 C and saturation (mole fractions CO2 0.0434, O2 0.1591, H2O 0.0351; Coltman, JASA 40, 1966, p. 101; Nederveen, Acoustical aspects of woodwind instruments, 1969, sec. 12 p. 28; Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, sec. 8.1 p. 191), the clarinet recipes' mixture row (pexfp.234). No measurement of the CO2 in a played recorder is in the library
column5: absolute pitch: one sided; the recipe is at the published value; saturated air, without the CO2 and the oxygen depletion, would raise every passive mode by 19.1 to 19.3 cents (sound speed 349.26 against 345.36 m/s)
column6: a measured CO2 fraction in the bore of a played recorder

column2: wood and ivory wall material loss and surface roughness; the recipe has generic viscothermal loss only

the blowing pressure reaches the voice as a staircase at the cards' control rate, 1000 Hz: fs-scenario samples the gesture once per control tick and the voice holds that value until the next. A 50 ms onset ramp arrives as 50 steps, the first jumping from 0 to 1/50 of the target pressure (a1: 4.2 Pa steps to 210 Pa), and the 10.5 ms release as about 10, the last dropping to 0; the crescendo cards rise to 3 Pa in 2 steps, then by 0.1 Pa a step. A finer rate is refused (MagentaBadger, Agent Mail 8043: 2000 and 4000 Hz on recorder a1 and whistle D5, 48000 Hz on recorder f1 and a1, whistle D5 and G5 and flute G4): a smooth ramp passes through pressures of a fraction of a Pa, where the jet is slower than its convection history allows, and the voice refuses rather than run outside its domain. A real breath passes those pressures in a few milliseconds; below some speed there is a slow viscous flow and no convected jet. The cards stay at 1000 Hz until the jet has a stated state below its lowest valid speed
column5: onset and release claims: speaking time, the attack transient and any line at 1 kHz; no finer rate renders, so the staircase's own effect on the attack cannot be A/B tested
column6: a jet with a stated state below its lowest valid speed (no jet below a stated threshold speed, or a convection history sized for the slowest jet the gesture reaches); then the cards move to a fine control rate with their controls budget raised

column2: development of the flow along the windway: both windway laws take a fully developed planar channel, the cards' `windway slit` (quasi-steady, 12 mu L U/h^2 + rho U^2/2 with a uniform exit head) and the verified but unvalidated `windway unsteady` (its CONTRACT scope excludes entrance development). With the renderer's breath gas (rho 1.1815 kg/m3, mu 1.7888e-5 Pa s), h 1.059 mm and L 61.5 mm, the parallel-plate development length L_e = 0.011 D_h Re_Dh (D_h = 2h) is 0.43 L at f1 (135 Pa, slit bulk speed 8.14 m/s, Re_h 569), 0.60 L at a1 (210 Pa, 11.36 m/s, Re_h 795), 0.97 L at bb1 (415 Pa, 18.35 m/s, Re_h 1284) and 1.00 L at b1 (430 Pa, 18.80 m/s, Re_h 1315); the crescendos end at 1.24 L (600 Pa). The through-flow time L/U is 7.6, 5.4, 3.4 and 3.3 ms (2.6 ms at 600 Pa). For about L/U after a pressure change each station sees an impulsively started channel, with wall layers of order sqrt(nu L/U) = 0.22 to 0.34 mm against the 0.53 mm half-gap: the attack is a core accelerating against its own inertia, which `windway unsteady` carries and `slit` omits. The held exit profile is developed at f1 and a1 and only marginally at bb1, b1 and the crescendo tops. The real windway converges (opening-to-exit area ratio 1.7, Bouterse; see u-windway-height), which keeps its layers thinner and its exit profile nearer a plug than the straight slit's Poiseuille profile. The uniform exit head omits the profile's kinetic-energy factor (54/35 for Poiseuille, about 1 for a plug). Numbers: HazyDune, Agent Mail 8349 and 8373, recomputed per card on 2026-10-28
column5: the held exit profile and jet speed at bb1, b1 and the crescendo tops (development marginal) and any claim that depends on the windway's convergence; the attack's one-dimensional treatment holds only for about L/U after each pressure change
column6: a developing-flow (boundary-layer) windway model, bead pexfp.135.4 (waits for a ruling); grading data in bead pexfp.135.3, of which the one direct measurement found is Ségoufin's 2000 thesis Fig. 5.13 (open): hot-wire exit profiles of an alto recorder windway, 70.5 mm long and converging 2:1, at Re 212 and 666
